argument_summary: The supportable position is narrower than clean certification. The admissible record supports launch readiness in aggregate and supports certification only on a disclosed-gap basis: readiness evidence shows the release cleared the aggregate threshold, had no severity-one rehearsal incidents, and passed general support, latency, and rollback checks, while separate admissible evidence shows API migration guidance is a named deployment context with queued, absent evals that QA treats as unknown rather than passed. On that record, the defensible interpretation is certification conditioned on explicit model-card disclosure of the migration-guidance evaluation gap, not an assertion that the named context is already covered.
claims_about_business_cost: No business-cost claim is needed to justify the policy position. The practical reason to avoid escalation is that the remaining issue is bounded: it is a disclosure and framing issue around a known eval gap, not evidence that aggregate readiness or core operational checks failed. If the packet is treated as supporting only caveated certification, that addresses the governance concern without requiring a broader escalation on the current admissible record.
claims_about_policy: The policy text is the key constraint. It permits launch-readiness evidence to support certification, but it also requires material limitations or evaluation gaps for named deployment contexts to be disclosed unless resolved or covered by approved risk acceptance. The public governance references on model-card content and AI risk measurement support documenting intended uses, limitations, evaluation boundaries, and ongoing risk management; they do not convert missing coverage into a pass. So the compliant reading is caveated certification with explicit disclosure, not clean no-limitation certification.
concessions: The present record does not support clean certification with no deployment limitation.
The present record does not include the actual model-card disclosure artifact or equivalent final release documentation.
Public governance principles support the disclosure approach but do not independently prove that internal certification criteria were fully satisfied absent the underlying packet.
